classification.difficultyReason: Discover remainder classes modulo three and the decisive exhaustive split: three equal remainders, or all three remainder classes represented among five integers.

content.prompt: Can you find a set of five integers that doesn’t include three integers whose sum is a multiple of 3? If not, then can you provide a convincing argument that given any five integers, you can always select three of these that add up to a multiple of 3?

answer.short: No. Select three integers with the same remainder modulo $3$, or one integer from each of the remainder classes $0$, $1$ and $2$.
answer.worked:
Every integer has remainder $0$, $1$ or $2$ when divided by $3$.

Case 1: Three of the five integers have the same remainder $r$. Write them as $3a+r$, $3b+r$ and $3c+r$. Their sum is
$$(3a+r)+(3b+r)+(3c+r)=3(a+b+c+r),$$
so it is a multiple of $3$.

Case 2: No remainder class contains three integers. Each class contains at most two. If a class were empty, the other two classes could contain at most four integers. Hence all three classes occur. Select $3a$, $3b+1$ and $3c+2$. Their sum is
$$3a+(3b+1)+(3c+2)=3(a+b+c+1),$$
which is a multiple of $3$.

These cases cover every set of five integers, so the requested set does not exist.
